name: Tilly and the Midsummer Run
description: On the shortest night of the year, the night train takes an extra, secret stop at a meadow full of fireflies, and Tilly discovers the best part of the journey.

chapters.title: The Shortest Night
text: Midsummer is the shortest night of the year, so short that the sun only goes down for a quick nap before it is up again. On that night, the little train named Marigold left Hollow Station with every window open, and a warm, sweet wind blowing through all her carriages.

Tilly the hedgehog stood at the door with her ticket punch. She wore her lightest scarf, a tiny straw hat and a small bunch of clover behind one ear. "Good evening," she said, to each passenger. "Mind the step. It is a lovely night."

It was. The sky was apricot and violet, and the hills rolled away on either side, dotted with sleepy sheep. The passengers climbed aboard: the bear in his nightcap, with a very large straw fan, the owl with her book, the two rabbits with a picnic basket and, quite unexpectedly, the mole, who had never before been out in the open air after dark.
"I came for the fireflies," he said, a little shyly, pushing up his spectacles. "I have never seen one. I hear they are very good."

chapters.title: The Long Light
text: Marigold chuffed along beside a wide, slow river, and the light, instead of fading, stayed golden and long, spilling across the meadows. The rabbits opened their picnic basket and passed around cold lemonade and strawberry sandwiches. The bear ate seven, and said they were small.

Tilly walked the length of the train, humming. She stopped at each window to look out. A farmer waved from a field. A family of swans sailed under a bridge. A small dog ran alongside the train for a hundred yards, tongue out, delighted, and then stopped to roll in the grass.

"Does the train always go this way?" asked the mole. "Almost," said Tilly. "But on Midsummer night, Marigold takes a secret turning. She does not tell anyone where. She just slows down, at a certain place, and waits."
The mole looked out of the window with wide, hopeful eyes. "I do not mind waiting," he said. "I have been waiting for fireflies all my life."

chapters.title: The Secret Turning
text: Just as the sky turned from gold to rose, Marigold slowed, and left the main line, bumping gently over a little wooden crossing that Tilly had never seen before. The track curved through a stand of tall, whispering birches, and then, with a soft sigh, the train rolled out into a wide, hidden meadow.

It was very quiet. The grass was long and silver in the dusk, and the air smelled of honey and cut hay. Marigold stopped, with a final, gentle "chuff," and her whole body seemed to relax, like a person sitting down at the end of a long day.

"Here?" whispered the mole. "Here," said Tilly. She slid open the door, and the passengers stepped down, one at a time, onto the soft grass. They did not talk. There was nothing, at that moment, that needed saying.
And then, from the far edge of the meadow, a single small light blinked on.

chapters.title: Fireflies
text: One firefly, then three, then a dozen, then so many that Tilly lost count. They rose out of the grass like sparks from a campfire, and drifted up, and spread, and blinked, and by the time the stars came out, the whole meadow was glittering, as if the sky had spilled itself on the ground.

The mole did not move. He stood in the long grass, with his spectacles shining, and his mouth a little open. A firefly landed on his nose, and glowed, and he whispered, "Oh." It was the only thing he said for a very long time.

The bear lay down on his back in the grass with his hands on his stomach. The rabbits sat with their ears twitching. The owl closed her book, which she did not do for just anything. And Tilly, who had seen the fireflies every year, found that she had never really looked at them before.

"They are talking," said the mole, at last. "Look. They are blinking in a pattern. It is like a language." Tilly watched. It was true. The lights went on and off in slow, patient rhythms, as if the meadow were telling a very old, very kind story.

chapters.title: The Best Part
text: They stayed in the meadow until the sky began to lighten. When Marigold gave a quiet whistle, the passengers rose, one at a time, brushing grass from their coats. Nobody wanted to go, and nobody complained.

The mole walked back to the train very slowly, holding a single firefly in his cupped hands. At the door, he opened them, and it rose, and rejoined the others. "Thank you," he said, to no one in particular. "I did not know there were such things."

Tilly settled into the luggage rack as Marigold rolled quietly back through the birches, onto the main line, and into the pale morning. "Marigold," she whispered, "I think I have worked out what the best part of the journey is." The train gave a soft, questioning puff.

"It is the part where nobody is in a hurry," said Tilly. "And you stop, and everyone looks at the same lovely thing, at the same time." Marigold hummed, a long, deep, contented hum. And the night train, shortest of all nights, carried everyone home.
